transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-03
Time: 15:00 PT
Duration: ~49 minutes
Attendees: Alex Carter (Redwood AE), Priya Sharma (Redwood SE), Jordan Li (Redwood Solutions), Maya Ortiz (CTO, Zenith), Ethan Park (Head of ML), Sofia Ramos (PM), Liam Chen (Infra)

[00:00] Alex: Hey everyone thanks for joining, I'm Alex from Redwood, I'm the AE for this account, with me is Priya our solutions engineer and Jordan will hop in on infra questions, how's everyone doing?
[00:12] Maya: Doing good, thanks Alex, excited to learn more - we've been evaluating model options for a month now.
[00:20] Ethan: Yeah hi all, quick context - Zenith is building a multilingual virtual assistant and a docs summarization pipeline that needs to handle long contracts up to 80k tokens, and also call external tools (calendar, db queries). We're trying to figure out which model and deployment mode makes sense: hosted, dedicated, or private.
[00:40] Priya: Great, that's exactly what we help with. A couple quick qualification q's - what's your target latency and throughput? Also any compliance/regulatory constraints?
[00:50] Sofia: Latency target is p90 < 800ms for short chat interactions (2-3 turns) and for document ops we can tolerate higher, like 2-3s. Throughput is modest today ~20 concurrent users, but we expect spike loads during business hours, maybe up to 200 concurrent. Compliance wise: we need SOC 2, SSO via SAML, and customer-managed KMS for private deployments; some customers want EU data residency.
[01:18] Alex: Those are helpful. To confirm, long-context 80k tokens is a hard requirement for some use cases?
[01:24] Ethan: For contract summarization yes — we need to keep full context in many cases. For chat, 32k is fine, but the contract pipeline should support at least 80k or provide a RAG pattern that handles it transparently.
[01:36] Priya: Good. On model selection, we usually compare a few open models and variants — for large context you can go with models that support 32k natively and either chunk + RAG for 80k or use our extended context flow with models that support 128k. There are tradeoffs in latency/cost.
[01:52] Maya: Can you give concrete model examples? We've looked at Llama2-based variants, Mistral, and some 4x merged long-context models, and of course OpenAI's 32k/128k offerings.
[02:05] Priya: Sure — for open-source options we recommend (depending on workload): Llama 2 70B quantized variants for cost-effective generation, Mistral-based models for latency, and some newer long-context optimized models (we call them "LC" variants) that extend kv cache to 128k. Quick note: transcription may mislabel model names sometimes — we say Lama2 sometimes, but it's Llama.
[02:28] Ethan: Haha, noted. For tool-calling we need function-style tool invocation (structured outputs), plus the assistant must call our calendar API and a DB read API with auth. Is that supported?
[02:40] Priya: Yes, Redwood supports structured tool calling and function-style outputs. For Hosted we provide secure outbound integrations and you can proxy through your VPC for dedicated/private. We also provide tokenized auth patterns and can integrate with your OAuth or service tokens. In private deployments you keep control of keys and outbound networking.
[03:02] Liam: On networking — if we go private, we need on-prem or VPC with strict egress rules and HSM/KMS integration. Is HSM supported?
[03:10] Jordan: We support KMS/HSM integrations for private deployments; typically we integrate with AWS KMS, GCP KMS or an HSM via customer-managed key store. There are a couple of configuration options, we can share the ops doc.
[03:22] Maya: Security wise, do you have SOC 2 and pen test reports? Our procurement will need that.
[03:27] Alex: Yes we have SOC 2 Type II and we can share redacted pen test reports and our security pack. I'll send those after the call.
[03:35] Sofia: Awesome. Back to model tradeoffs — how do you recommend we approach latency vs cost for the chat (32k) vs the contract pipeline (80k)?
[03:44] Priya: For chat, if you need low-latency p90 under 800ms, we'd typically suggest a smaller Llama2 70B quantized or a Mistral variant on Dedicated to get the predictable latency. Hosted can also hit it but at higher cost per token unless you use caching and batching. For the contract pipeline, there are two patterns: 1) use a long-context model (128k LC variant) in Dedicated/Private to keep everything in-context — simpler but more expensive per token; 2) use chunking + RAG with an embedding index and a dense retriever, which offloads most tokens to the retriever and only sends condensed context to the model — cheaper and often faster overall, but adds complexity.
[04:18] Ethan: We prefer simpler pipelines where possible. If the long-context model on Dedicated meets cost targets, that's ideal. Do you have benchmark numbers for 80k context runs?
[04:27] Priya: We have internal benchmarks and can run a pilot. Typical numbers: long-context models on Dedicated with GPU-optimized runtime can keep generation latency for single-turn summaries in the 1.5-3s range depending on sequence length and hardware. For big 80k summarizations you'll see higher end. We'll propose a benchmark run on your sample docs so you can see p50/p90.
[04:46] Maya: That would be great — we can share a small set of redacted contracts.
[04:50] Alex: Perfect — action item for Ethan to share sample prompts and docs.
[04:54] Ethan: Will do.
[04:57] Sofia: How does function/tool calling work across hosted vs private? Any differences in latency or reliability?
[05:05] Priya: Mechanically it's the same API and function schema. For Hosted, calls go through Redwood's control plane with secure connections; Dedicated routes through customer-dedicated capacity but still uses Redwood control plane for routing unless you opt for Private where the control plane is customer-managed. Private reduces external egress for sensitive data and gives you direct network control which can improve compliance but may add operational overhead. Latency differences are usually dominated by network hops; Dedicated in the same region as your users is often best for predictable latency.
[05:37] Liam: About multilinguism — our assistant needs to handle Spanish, Portuguese, Japanese and Korean at high quality. Any model you recommend?
[05:45] Priya: For multilingual, choose models trained with a strong multilingual corpus or use specialized finetunes. Some Llama variants are decent, but certain Mistral and community long-context models have better multilingual performance. Additionally, you can layer small finetunes on top or use instruction tuning for your domain. We'll share a short comparison matrix.
[06:05] Maya: Do you do model fine-tuning or RLHF?
[06:09] Alex: Redwood doesn't provide RLHF as a hosted service by default — we help customers with finetuning workflows and can integrate open-source toolchains; many customers do small supervised finetunes or instruction-tuning offline and then serve the finetuned artifact via Dedicated or Private.
[06:23] Ethan: Licensing — for dedicated and private do you require any special model licenses? We often care about MLR/LLM licensing for some commercial models.
[06:31] Priya: We support open models and we help track license compatibility. For hosted we curate model variants we know are safe to serve. If you have specific licensing constraints we can advise and recommend permissive open models.
[06:44] Sofia: Pricing question — can you ballpark hosted vs dedicated?
[06:48] Alex: Ballpark: Hosted is pay-as-you-go per token; costs vary by model footprint (smaller models cheaper). Dedicated is a committed monthly capacity — higher fixed cost but lower unit token price and predictable latency. Private has platform fees plus infra. I'll send a concrete sheet with examples.
[07:02] Priya: Also worth calling out Redwood Optimize — it can recommend batching, quantization, and caching profiles to cut unit costs by 20-60% depending on workloads.
[07:12] Maya: Good to know. For the pilot, would we run it on Hosted or Dedicated?
[07:16] Alex: Usually pilot on Hosted for speed, or a short Dedicated trial if you need consistent latency measurements. For security-sensitive samples we can run a private pilot in your VPC. We'll aim to propose options.
[07:29] Ethan: For the benchmark harness — what do you need from us?
[07:33] Priya: Sample prompt set, typical user flows, a set of redacted contracts for full-context runs, and target SLOs. We'll provide a harness (notebook + scripts) that runs p50/p90 latency and quality metrics and shares the raw logs.
[07:49] Maya: Ok we'll assemble that and get to you by Friday.
[07:52] Alex: Great. A couple quick clarifying q's from procurement perspective — SSO/SAML, audit logs retention, and data deletion policies?
[07:59] Maya: Procurement will need all that before legal signs off.
[08:03] Alex: We'll include those in the security pack. Also, competitors — have you run benchmarks vs OpenAI or Anthropic?
[08:11] Ethan: We've done some internal comparisons with OpenAI 32k and some Anthropic runs; we want to see comparable latency and cost with open models.
[08:20] Priya: Understood — we'll include a competitor comparison sheet and our benchmark methodology. For long-context there's often a noticeable cost delta if you keep everything in-context vs RAG.
[08:33] Sofia: Any gotchas on embeddings or retrieval size for the RAG approach?
[08:38] Priya: Retrieval quality depends on embedding model and index strategy. For multilingual corpora we recommend language-aware embeddings or cross-lingual models. Index sharding and vector DB tuning matter — we can share recommendations based on your data sizes.
[08:55] Liam: On infra — if we pick Dedicated, what's the typical lead time for provisioning capacity?
[09:00] Alex: Typical lead time is 2-4 weeks depending on region and spec. Dedicated setup includes capacity reservation and some infra config; we can fast-track in some cases. Private on-prem is longer.
[09:12] Maya: Timeline wise we're hoping to decide by mid-November and run a pilot in late November. Does that fit with your provisioning?
[09:20] Alex: Yes that's doable.
[09:22] Priya: We'll put together a proposed timeline in the follow-up.
[09:26] [Cross talk — brief logistics about calendar invites] 
[09:40] Alex: Ok to wrap up, recap: We'll send pricing + SLA + security pack; Priya will send benchmark harness; Ethan will share sample prompts and docs; schedule tech deep-dive for Nov 10. Any other items?
[09:54] Maya: That's it from us. Thanks.
[10:00] Alex: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up.

Notes: transcript contains minor transcription errors / name swaps typical of automated tools. References: shared deck (link: https://redwood.ai/decks/zenith-model-selection), benchmark harness repo (link provided by Priya during call).
